what: Re-derived TRUE Bundle.entry resourceTypes for all 8 FHIR use cases. The compiled spec had put PROFILE names and row LABELS in the resourceType slot. Every corrected value is derived from, in order: the row's profile URL resolved through constants.json fhirProfiles, the row's guidance sentence, the ./resourceType fixed value on the resource's own Confluence page, and finally the official sample.

resourceTypeDerivation: 2. row guidance sentence (‘SHALL be set to …’ / ‘entry of type …’), with trailing prose words such as ‘Resource’ stripped
3. the resource page's own ./resourceType fixed value (constants.json resourceTypes, 24 entries)
4. the official sample as final arbiter
method.labelsAreNotTypes: A row label such as ‘Bundle entry(s) for Imaging Procedure’ names the CLINICAL ROLE of the entry. The FHIR resourceType is whatever the profile constrains — here Procedure. Nine of the sixteen phantoms were exactly this mistake.
method.orderNotEnforcedBeyondFirst: Only entry[0] has a stated ordering rule. Sample entry order diverges from table order in the radiology report bundles, so the ordered lists below are DECLARATION order, not a wire-order constraint.

Searched all four document Bundle pages (351502348, 63701020, 387645441, 413728794) for the phrase ‘first entry’: zero hits, whereas 44008229 and 118161740 return it twice each. conflicts.investigation: Both governing Confluence pages — 44139001 (uncontrolled) and 118161707 (Raqeeb) — state bundleDispense|1.0 identically, in the same row 1.1 and with identical wording. The wire value .../medicationdispensed|1.0 is NOT an unknown URL: constants.json fhirProfiles already binds it to resourceType Medication, sourced from pages 118161914 and 47054851 (‘Medication: Dispensed Medicinal Product or Compound’). DECISIVE EVIDENCE: inside every one of the four affected samples the SAME URL .../medicationdispensed|1.0 also appears, correctly, as the meta.profile of the CONTAINED Medication resource within MedicationDispense. One URL cannot profile both a Bundle and a Medication, so the Bundle-level occurrence is a copy/paste defect in the published samples, not an undocumented alternative. The prescription counterparts are the control: their bundles correctly carry bundlePrescription|1.0 while their contained Medication carries medicationprescribed|1.0.
conflicts.recommendation: Keep bundleDispense|1.0 as the fixed value for Bundle.meta.profile on both dispense use cases. A workbench MUST NOT silently accept medicationdispensed|1.0 as correct, but SHOULD downgrade it from a hard error to a named warning that says: ‘this is the profile of the contained Medication resource, not of the Bundle — all four official NPHIES dispense samples carry this defect, so a receiving system may tolerate it’. Escalate to NPHIES to have the four sample files corrected.

specSources.quote: Exactly one entry of type “Composition (structured)” SHALL be present, representing the “document-view” of the Radiology Report information.

conflicts.investigation: The sample is unambiguously the STRUCTURED variant: its Composition carries six coded, titled sections (Imaging Study, Clinical Information, Procedures, Comparison / Previous Findings, Procedure findings, Impressions) and its bundle carries ImagingStudy, Procedure(.../ImagingProcedure|1.0), Binary and Endpoint entries — all structured-only rows — and no DocumentReference. Yet entry[0].meta.profile is compositionRadReportEmbeddedPDF|1.0. The embedded-PDF sample by contrast has two sections and a DocumentReference, matching its profile.
conflicts.recommendation: Treat compositionRadReportStructured|1.0 as correct for the structured variant. Because variant selection keys off this profile, a workbench should fall back to shape-based variant detection (presence of DocumentReference → embedded PDF; presence of Procedure/Binary/Endpoint → structured) rather than trusting the profile URL alone. Report the mismatch to NPHIES as a sample defect.

specSources.quote: Exactly one entry of type “Diagnostic Report” SHALL be present, representing the “data-view” of the Radiology Report information.

conflicts.investigation: Page 414154754 makes DiagnosticReport mandatory for the structured variant, and page 414744577 defines the profile .../diagnosticreportRadReport|1.0 for it. The only official structured sample has no DiagnosticReport entry at all. The embedded-PDF table (414679041) has no DiagnosticReport row, so its absence there is correct. Note the parallel: the Laboratory Report bundle makes the same document-view/data-view pairing mandatory and all 3 lab-report samples DO carry the DiagnosticReport — which argues the radiology sample, not the radiology spec, is at fault.
conflicts.recommendation: Keep DiagnosticReport as M [1..1] for the structured variant (quoted, and corroborated by the analogous lab-report rule), but flag it at reduced severity until a second official structured sample is published: a single sample is not enough to overturn a verbatim SHALL. Ask NPHIES whether DiagnosticReport is genuinely mandatory for structured radiology reports or whether row 2 of 414154754 is stale.

specSources.quote: One to many entry(s) of type “Service Request” SHALL be present.

conflicts.investigation: constants.json fhirProfiles carries two ServiceRequest profiles: servicerequestLabReport (page 67993727, the Laboratory Report row) and servicerequest (page 358580229, the Laboratory Orders row). All 3 official lab-report samples send the ORDERS profile .../servicerequest|1.0 on their six ServiceRequest entries. The resourceType is not in question — only which profile URL is normative for this row.
conflicts.recommendation: Do NOT enforce servicerequestLabReport|1.0 as a fixed value on this row. Record both URLs as acceptable and surface the divergence as informational, because a lab-report ServiceRequest is in practice the very ServiceRequest that was ordered. Confirm with NPHIES which profile a receiving validator actually asserts. This is out of scope for the entry-resourceType gate but was found while reconciling and would otherwise become the next false positive.
